subLevels.reveal: Well done! Several of these were named after the same Germanic gods, e.g. "Thor" for "Thursday" is the god of thunder, which is Donner in German.

subLevels.reveal: Nice! This was originally "Wodanstag", but early Germanic-speaking Christian missionaries tried to remove the pagan god names from the days of the week...and succeeded only with this one.

hints.hint: von was sometimes used in aristocratic names to indicate where they were from. For example, Manfred von Richthofen was the WWI flying ace the Red Baron.

subLevels.reveal: The English word "noon" comes from Latin "nona" (ninth hour (after sunrise), i.e. 3 pm). The medieval prayer None was held then, but its associated meal crept earlier over centuries, winding up at midday and lending its name to the hour.

subLevels.reveal: Germans celebrate the end of their workweek with the phrase Feierabend, literally "celebration evening". Colleagues often mark it with a Feierabendbier!
Sonntage are sacred in Germany, with most stores including supermarkets and even some restaurants closing for the day, a tradition called Sonntagsruhe ("Sunday quiet").
